intro: Buddhists often say the Buddha's teaching fits in a few lists. There are Four Noble Truths, an Eightfold Path and five precepts. Children in Buddhist families often learn these lists early, the way other kids learn a pledge or a prayer.

In this unit you will learn what these teachings say, as Buddhists explain them. You will read about dukkha, craving and nirvana. You will see how the Eightfold Path is grouped. You will learn what karma and rebirth mean in Buddhist teaching.

Then you will read short verses from the Dhammapada. You will compare translations and see how families use the verses in daily life. By the end, you will be able to explain the core teachings and cite the texts they come from.
bigQuestion: What do the Buddha's core teachings say, and how do Buddhists live by them?

Buddhist families in Illinois recite the precepts and learn Dhammapada verses.

title: Key Teachings

chapters.title: Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path
chapters.bigQuestion: What are the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path, and how do Buddhists explain them?

story.title: Four Questions at the Clinic
story.kicker: A doctor looks at a sick patient and asks four questions in a row.
paragraphs: Dr. Patel's clinic is busy on Monday morning. A boy named Leo sits on the paper-covered table. His throat hurts. His mom sits in the chair beside him, holding his jacket.
Dr. Patel listens closely. First she asks herself, "What is wrong?" She looks in his throat. It is red and sore. That is the problem. Leo waits and watches her face.
Next she asks, "What is causing it?" She runs a quick test. It is an infection. Then she asks, "Can it be cured?" She smiles at Leo. "Yes, it can." Leo lets out a breath.
Last she asks, "What will cure it?" She writes a plan: medicine, rest and lots of water. Leo's mom tucks the paper into her purse. Leo hops off the table, already feeling a little better.
Many Buddhist teachers use a picture like this one. They say the Buddha taught like a good doctor. His Four Noble Truths follow the same four steps: the problem, the cause, the cure and the plan.
story.think: Why might a teacher compare a religious teaching to a doctor's visit?

lessons.title: The First Truth: Dukkha
lessons.mainIdea: The first noble truth, Buddhists teach, is that life includes dukkha: suffering, stress and dissatisfaction.
reading: In his first sermon, the Buddha taught four truths. Buddhists call them the Four Noble Truths. The first is about *dukkha*. Dukkha is a Pali word. It is often translated as suffering.

Dukkha covers more than pain. It includes sickness, old age and loss. It includes not getting what you want. It includes the feeling that nothing lasts. Some translators use words like stress or unsatisfactoriness.
The first sermon lists many kinds of dukkha. Birth, aging, sickness and death are among them. Buddhists say naming the problem clearly is the first step, just as a doctor names an illness.

words.d: suffering, stress or dissatisfaction; the first noble truth
fine and worthy of honor

look.title: One Word, Many Meanings
look.text: Translators put dukkha into English many ways: suffering, pain, stress, dissatisfaction, unsatisfactoriness. Each word catches part of the meaning. None catches all of it.
look.prompt: Which English word do you think fits best? Why is choosing hard?

check.q: What does dukkha usually mean in English?
check.why: Dukkha is often translated as suffering, stress or dissatisfaction.

check.q: Which noble truth is about dukkha?
check.why: The first noble truth names dukkha.

check.q: In the doctor picture, the first truth is like...
check.why: Naming the problem is like the first noble truth.

lessons.title: The Second Truth: Craving
lessons.mainIdea: The second noble truth, Buddhists teach, is that dukkha comes from craving.
reading: The second noble truth names the cause of dukkha. The Pali word is *tanha*. It means thirst or *craving*. Buddhists say it is the grasping wish for things to be different than they are.
The first sermon names three kinds of craving. There is craving for pleasures. There is craving to be or become something. There is craving to get rid of things.
Buddhists say craving is like a thirst that is never satisfied. When one want is met, a new one appears. The second truth, like a doctor's test, finds the cause.

words.d: a strong, grasping want; tanha in Pali
Pali for thirst or craving, the cause of dukkha in Buddhist teaching

look.title: The Next New Toy
look.text: A girl wants a new game for weeks. She gets it and plays all day. A week later, she sees a newer game in an ad. Now she wants that one.
look.prompt: How might a Buddhist teacher use this example to explain craving?

check.q: What does tanha mean?
check.why: Tanha is Pali for thirst or craving.

check.q: What does the second noble truth name?
check.why: The second truth names craving as the cause.

check.q: Which is one kind of craving named in the first sermon?
check.why: The sermon names craving for pleasures, for becoming and for getting rid of things.

lessons.title: The Third and Fourth Truths
lessons.mainIdea: The third truth says dukkha can end, in nirvana; the fourth names the path that leads there.
reading: The third noble truth says dukkha can end. When craving stops, Buddhists teach, dukkha stops too. This ending is called *nirvana* (Pali: nibbana). The word means blowing out, like a flame.
Buddhists describe nirvana as peace and freedom. They say it is hard to put into words. Different schools explain it in different ways. Some describe it as the highest happiness.
The fourth noble truth names the way to get there. It is the Noble Eightfold Path. In the doctor picture, the third truth says "there is a cure." The fourth is the treatment plan.

words.d: "blowing out"; the end of dukkha in Buddhist teaching (Pali: nibbana)
a way to travel; in Buddhism, a way of living and practice

look.title: The Four Truths as a Doctor's Visit
look.cite: Samyutta Nikaya 56.11; the medical comparison is a common teaching image
look.prompt: Which truth matches the treatment plan?

check.q: What does nirvana mean literally?
check.why: Nirvana means blowing out, like a flame.

check.q: What does the fourth noble truth name?
check.why: The fourth truth is the path that leads to the end of dukkha.

check.q: What is the Pali form of nirvana?
check.why: Nirvana is Sanskrit; nibbana is Pali.

lessons.title: Eight Parts, Three Groups
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists often sort the eight parts of the path into three groups: wisdom, ethics and meditation.
reading: The *Eightfold Path* has eight parts. Each begins with the word right, or wise. They are right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness and concentration.

Buddhist teachers often sort them into three groups. Wisdom includes right view and right intention. Ethics includes right speech, action and livelihood. Meditation includes right effort, mindfulness and concentration.
Buddhists say the parts work together, not one at a time. They compare them to strands of a rope. Each part makes the others stronger. No single part is the whole path.

words.d: the eight-part way of living that Buddhists say leads to the end of dukkha
ideas about right and wrong ways to act

look.title: The Three Groups
look.unit: parts of the path in each group
look.cite: Majjhima Nikaya 44 (Culavedalla Sutta), which groups the path this way
look.prompt: Which group has the fewest parts?

check.q: How many parts does the path have?
check.why: The Noble Eightfold Path has eight parts.

check.q: Right speech belongs to which group?
check.why: Right speech, action and livelihood are grouped as ethics.

check.q: Right view belongs to which group?
check.why: Right view and right intention are grouped as wisdom.

lessons.title: Right Speech and Right Action
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists describe right speech and right action as not harming others with words or deeds.
reading: Right speech, the suttas say, means not lying, not speaking harshly, not gossiping to divide people and not chatting idly. Buddhists try to speak truthfully and kindly.
Right action means not killing, not stealing and not causing harm through sexual wrongdoing. Right livelihood means earning a living in a way that does not harm others.
Buddhist teachers say these parts shape everyday life. A Buddhist shopkeeper, nurse or student can practice them at work or school, not only in a temple.

words.d: speaking truthfully and kindly, one part of the Eightfold Path
the way a person earns a living

look.title: Words at Lunch
look.text: At lunch, a student hears a rumor about a classmate. She could pass it on. She could say something unkind. Or she could change the subject and say nothing hurtful.
look.prompt: Which choice fits right speech as the suttas describe it?

check.q: Which is part of right speech, say the suttas?
check.why: Right speech includes not lying and not speaking harshly.

check.q: What is livelihood?
choices: the way a person earns a living
check.why: Livelihood means how a person earns a living.

check.q: Where do teachers say people can practice right action?
check.why: Teachers say the path shapes everyday life at work and school.

lessons.title: Mindfulness and Concentration
lessons.mainIdea: The meditation group of the path includes effort, mindfulness and concentration, which Buddhists develop through practice.
reading: The last group is about training the mind. Right effort means working to grow good states of mind and let go of harmful ones. Buddhists describe it as steady, not strained.

Right *mindfulness* (sati in Pali) means paying clear attention to what is happening now. The Satipatthana Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 10, describes paying attention to the body, feelings, mind and teachings.

Right concentration means a calm, focused mind. The suttas describe deep states of meditation. In school we learn what Buddhists say about these practices. We describe them; we do not practice them in class.

words.d: clear attention to what is happening now; sati in Pali
a calm and focused mind

look.title: Four Places of Attention
look.text: The Buddha tells the monks there is one direct way to purify beings and end sorrow: the four foundations of mindfulness, which are body, feelings, mind and mental qualities.
look.prompt: What four things does this sutta say to pay attention to?

check.q: What is the Pali word for mindfulness?
check.why: Sati is Pali for mindfulness.

check.q: Which sutta describes the foundations of mindfulness?
check.why: The Satipatthana Sutta is Majjhima Nikaya 10.

check.q: What do we do with meditation in class?
choices: describe what Buddhists say about it
check.why: In a public school we describe practices; we do not lead them.

lessons.title: The Dharma Wheel
lessons.mainIdea: The eight-spoked Dharma wheel is a Buddhist symbol for the teaching and the Eightfold Path.
reading: The *Dharma wheel* (dharmachakra) is one of the oldest Buddhist symbols. It often has eight spokes. Buddhists say the spokes stand for the eight parts of the path.

The wheel also recalls the first sermon, "Setting the Wheel of the Dharma in Motion." A wheel rolls forward, like a teaching that spreads. Early Buddhist art often showed a wheel instead of a human figure of the Buddha.
Ashoka's pillars carried wheels. India's national flag today shows a wheel, the Ashoka Chakra, with 24 spokes. Buddhist temples around the world use the eight-spoked wheel.

words.d: an eight-spoked wheel that stands for the Buddha's teaching
a picture or object that stands for an idea

look.title: Counting Spokes
look.cite: Common Buddhist iconography; Flag of India (adopted 1947)
look.prompt: Why might the Buddhist wheel have exactly eight spokes?

check.q: What do the eight spokes stand for, Buddhists say?
check.why: Buddhists link the eight spokes to the Eightfold Path.

check.q: Which flag shows a wheel with 24 spokes?
check.why: India's flag shows the Ashoka Chakra with 24 spokes.

check.q: What is a symbol?
choices: a picture that stands for an idea
check.why: A symbol stands for an idea.

lessons.title: Karma
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists teach karma: intentional actions shape what happens to a person later.
reading: *Karma* (Pali: kamma) means action. Buddhists use it for intentional actions of body, speech and mind. A sutta has the Buddha say that intention itself is karma.
Buddhists teach that good actions tend to bring good results and harmful actions tend to bring harm. They compare it to seeds. What you plant grows later.
Buddhists do not usually describe karma as a judge handing out rewards. They describe it more like a natural pattern. Teachers from different schools explain it in different ways.

words.d: intentional action and its results, in Buddhist teaching (Pali: kamma)
what you mean or plan to do

look.title: Planting Seeds
look.text: A gardener plants tomato seeds in spring. Weeks later, tomatoes grow, not roses. Buddhist teachers often use this picture. They say actions are like seeds that bring matching fruit.
look.prompt: What does the seed picture suggest about karma, as Buddhists explain it?

check.q: What does karma mean?
check.why: Karma means action, especially intentional action.

check.q: What picture do Buddhist teachers often use for karma?
check.why: Teachers compare actions to seeds that bring matching fruit.

check.q: What is the Pali form of karma?
check.why: Karma is Sanskrit; kamma is Pali.

lessons.title: Rebirth
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists traditionally teach rebirth: beings are born again and again until they reach nirvana.
reading: Most Buddhist traditions teach *rebirth*. They say beings are born again and again. This cycle of births is called samsara, "wandering on." The Jatakas and many sutras refer to it.
Buddhists say karma shapes what kind of rebirth a being has. The Jatakas show this idea. They tell of the Buddha's many earlier lives as animals and people.

Buddhists say nirvana ends the cycle. Some modern Buddhists, especially in the West, read rebirth in other ways, such as moment to moment. Views differ, and many Buddhists hold the traditional teaching.

words.d: being born again after death, as most Buddhist traditions teach
"wandering on"; the cycle of birth, death and rebirth in Buddhist teaching

look.title: The Wheel of Life
look.text: Tibetan temple doors often show a big round painting called the Wheel of Life. A fierce figure holds the wheel. Inside are pictures of different kinds of births. Outside, the Buddha points to the moon, a way out.
look.prompt: What might a visitor learn about samsara from this painting?

check.q: What is samsara?
choices: the cycle of birth and rebirth
check.why: Samsara means wandering on, the cycle of rebirth.

check.q: Which texts show the Buddha's many earlier lives?
check.why: The Jatakas tell of the Buddha's earlier lives.

check.q: What do Buddhists say ends the cycle of rebirth?
check.why: Buddhists teach that reaching nirvana ends samsara.

review.q: What is the first noble truth about?

review.why: The second truth names craving, tanha, as the cause.

review.q: In the doctor picture, which truth is the treatment?
review.why: The fourth truth, the Eightfold Path, is like the treatment plan.

review.q: Which of these is in the wisdom group?
review.why: Wisdom includes right view and right intention.
Buddhists take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma and Sangha.

chapters.title: Five Precepts and the Dhammapada's Sayings
chapters.bigQuestion: How do the five precepts and the Dhammapada's verses guide Buddhist everyday life?

story.title: A Verse on the Mirror
story.kicker: A girl copies one Dhammapada verse onto a card and tapes it to her mirror.
paragraphs: Linh is ten. Every Sunday her family goes to a Vietnamese Buddhist temple in Chicago. After the chanting, there is a class for kids. Today the teacher, a nun named Sister An, holds up a small green book.
"This is the Dhammapada," Sister An says. "It has 423 short verses. People have memorized them for a very long time." She reads one aloud, about hatred and love. The room is quiet for a moment.
At home, Linh takes an index card and a purple marker. She copies the verse in her neatest letters. She adds a small lotus in the corner. Then she tapes the card to her bedroom mirror.
The next week, her brother takes her headphones without asking. Linh feels her face get hot. She is about to yell. Then she sees the card on the mirror.
She takes a breath and walks to his room. "Can I have those back, please?" she asks. He hands them over. "Sorry," he mumbles. Linh thinks about the verse all afternoon.
story.think: Why might a short verse be easier to remember in a hard moment than a long talk?

lessons.title: Five Training Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Many Buddhist laypeople take five precepts, promises to train in not harming.
reading: Buddhist laypeople, people who are not monks or nuns, often take five *precepts*. A precept is a training rule. Buddhists usually say it as a promise: "I undertake the training rule to..."

The five are: not harming living beings, not taking what is not given, not misusing sex, not lying, and not taking drinks or drugs that cloud the mind. For children, the third is often explained as keeping faith and promises within families.
Buddhists recite the precepts at temples, often in Pali. They are the same in Theravada and Mahayana lands. Buddhists describe them as training, not commandments from a god.

words.d: a training rule or promise about how to live
a Buddhist who is not a monk or nun

look.title: The Five Precepts
rows: Not taking what is not given
Not misusing sex (keeping faith in families)
look.cite: The five precepts (pancasila), as listed in Anguttara Nikaya 8.39

check.q: How many precepts do Buddhist laypeople often take?
check.why: Laypeople often take five precepts; 227 is the monks' rule list.

check.q: What is a layperson?
choices: a Buddhist who is not a monk or nun
check.why: Laypeople live ordinary household lives.

check.q: How do Buddhists describe the precepts?
check.why: Buddhists describe them as training rules they take on.

lessons.title: Not Harming and Not Stealing
lessons.mainIdea: The first two precepts ask Buddhists not to harm living beings and not to take what is not given.
reading: The first precept is not harming living beings. Many Buddhists take this to mean animals and insects too. Some are vegetarian. Others are not, and traditions differ on food.
The second precept is not taking what is not given. It is wider than not stealing. It means not using or borrowing things without permission. Asking first is part of keeping it.
Buddhists often pair each precept with a good habit. With not harming goes kindness. With not taking goes generosity, or giving freely. Teachers say the good habit helps the promise grow.

words.d: giving freely to others
a person who does not eat meat

look.title: Borrowing a Pencil
look.text: Sam needs a pencil. His tablemate's pencil is right there. She is in the bathroom. Sam could just take it. Or he could wait and ask, or borrow one from the class bin.
look.prompt: How does the second precept, "not taking what is not given," apply here?

check.q: What is the second precept?
choices: not taking what is not given
check.why: The second precept is not taking what is not given.

check.q: Are all Buddhists vegetarian?
check.why: Some Buddhists are vegetarian; traditions differ on food.

check.q: Which good habit goes with not taking?
check.why: Teachers pair not taking with generosity.

lessons.title: Truth and a Clear Mind
lessons.mainIdea: The fourth and fifth precepts ask Buddhists to speak truthfully and keep the mind clear.
reading: The fourth precept is not lying. It connects to right speech on the Eightfold Path. Buddhists try to speak truthfully and kindly. Buddhists say kind truth builds trust.
The fifth precept is not taking drinks or drugs that cloud the mind. Buddhists explain it this way: a clouded mind makes it easier to break the other four.
Teachers say the five precepts protect others and the person who keeps them. When people keep promises, trust grows. Buddhists say a whole community becomes calmer.

words.d: a drink or drug that clouds the mind
believing someone will be honest and keep promises

look.title: Why Five Work Together
look.text: A Buddhist teacher might say: if your mind is clear, you notice before you say something unkind. If you tell the truth, people trust you. The precepts hold each other up, like legs of a table.
look.prompt: How does the fifth precept help with the other four?

check.q: Which precept is about lying?
check.why: The fourth precept is not lying.

check.q: Why do Buddhists say the fifth precept matters?
choices: a clouded mind breaks the others more easily
check.why: Buddhists say a clear mind helps keep all the precepts.

check.q: What is an intoxicant?
choices: a drink or drug that clouds the mind
check.why: An intoxicant clouds the mind.

lessons.title: A Book of Sayings
lessons.mainIdea: The Dhammapada is a collection of 423 short verses in 26 chapters, loved across the Buddhist world.
reading: The *Dhammapada* is in the Khuddaka Nikaya of the Pali Canon. Its 423 verses are grouped into 26 chapters. Chapters have titles like "Pairs," "The Mind," "Flowers" and "The Wise."
Buddhists memorize and chant its verses. Monks quote them in talks. Parents teach them to children. There are also early versions in other old Indian languages, and one in Chinese.
A later commentary tells a story for each verse. It says who the Buddha was speaking to and why. Kisa Gotami's story is told there. Teachers still retell these stories.

words.d: a Pali book of 423 short verses in 26 chapters
a short, well-known saying that gives advice

look.title: The Dhammapada by the Numbers
look.cite: Dhammapada, tr. F. Max Muller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10 (1881)
look.prompt: About how many verses are in each chapter, on average?

check.q: How many chapters does the Dhammapada have?
check.why: The Dhammapada has 26 chapters and 423 verses.

check.q: What does the Dhammapada commentary add?
check.why: The commentary tells why each verse was spoken.

check.q: What is a proverb?
choices: a short saying that gives advice
check.why: A proverb is a short, well-known saying.

lessons.title: The Mind Comes First
lessons.mainIdea: Dhammapada 1 and 2 teach, as Buddhists read them, that the mind shapes what we do and what follows.
reading: The Dhammapada opens with a pair of verses. Verse 1 says that when a person speaks or acts with a harmful mind, suffering follows. It compares this to a cart wheel following the ox that pulls it.
Verse 2 is its partner. It says that when a person acts with a pure mind, happiness follows, like a shadow that never leaves. Chapter 1 is called "Pairs" because its verses come in twos like this.
Buddhists read these verses as saying the *mind* comes first. Thoughts lead to words and deeds. Teachers link the verses to karma: actions made with intention bring results.

words.d: the part of a person that thinks, feels and chooses
two things that go together

look.title: Dhammapada, Verse 1
look.text: All that we are is the result of what we have thought: it is founded on our thoughts, it is made up of our thoughts.
look.cite: Dhammapada 1, tr. F. Max Muller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10 (1881)
look.prompt: Muller's words say we are "made up of" our thoughts. How would you say this in your own words?

check.q: What does verse 1 compare suffering to?
check.why: Verse 1 uses the wheel following the ox; verse 2 uses the shadow.

check.q: Why is chapter 1 called "Pairs"?
check.why: Chapter 1's verses come in matched pairs.

check.q: What do Buddhists say these verses teach?
check.why: Buddhists read verses 1 and 2 as showing the mind leads action.

lessons.title: Hatred and Love
lessons.mainIdea: Dhammapada 5 teaches, in Muller's translation, that hatred ceases by love.
reading: Dhammapada 5 is one of the most quoted Buddhist verses. It says hatred is never ended by more hatred. It is ended by its opposite. The verse calls this an old, lasting rule.
The commentary tells a story behind it. Two women kept harming each other's children through many lives. The Buddha taught them this verse so the cycle of revenge could stop.

Translators choose different words for what ends hatred. F. Max Muller wrote "love." Other translators use "non-hatred," "friendliness" or "kindness." The Pali word is *avera*, meaning without hatred or enmity.

words.d: a strong feeling of dislike and anger toward someone
Pali for non-hatred or non-enmity, the word in Dhammapada 5

look.title: Dhammapada, Verse 5
look.text: For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule.
look.cite: Dhammapada 5, tr. F. Max Muller, Sacred Books of the East vol. 10 (1881)
look.prompt: How did Linh in the story use this verse?

check.q: What ends hatred, in Muller's translation of verse 5?
check.why: Muller's 1881 translation says hatred ceases by love.

check.q: What is the Pali word in verse 5 that means non-hatred?
check.why: Avera means without hatred or enmity.

check.q: Why do translations of verse 5 differ?
check.why: Translators render avera as love, non-hatred, friendliness or kindness.

lessons.title: Memorizing and Chanting
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists memorize and chant Dhammapada verses, much as people keep proverbs.
reading: In Sri Lanka and Myanmar, many children learn Dhammapada verses in Sunday or Dhamma school. They memorize them in Pali and in their own language. Teachers help them say each line.
Adults quote them too. A verse can be written on a temple wall, printed on a calendar or spoken at a funeral. Buddhists say short verses are easy to carry in the mind.
Scholars note that the Dhammapada shares sayings with other old texts. Some verses are close to ones in Hindu and Jain books from the same time and region.

words.d: to learn something so well you can say it without looking
a class, often on Sundays, where Buddhist children learn teachings

look.title: Words on a Wall
look.text: In a temple courtyard, a verse is painted in large letters in two languages. Families walk past it every week. Children point to words they know. Grandparents read it aloud.
look.prompt: Why might a temple paint a verse where everyone walks by?

check.q: Where do many Buddhist children learn verses?
check.why: Many children learn verses in Sunday or Dhamma school.

check.q: What does memorize mean?
choices: learn so you can say it without looking

lessons.title: The Flower Chapter
lessons.mainIdea: The Dhammapada often uses pictures from nature, like flowers and bees, to teach.
reading: Chapter 4 of the Dhammapada is called "Flowers." Its verses use flower pictures. One verse compares a wise person in a village to a bee that takes nectar without hurting the flower.
Buddhists read this as a picture of monks who go for alms. They receive food from families, the teachers say, without being a burden, like a bee on a blossom.
The lotus also appears in Buddhist writing and art. It grows from mud but blooms clean above the water. Buddhists often use it as a sign of a pure mind rising from a hard world.

words.d: a water flower that grows from mud; a Buddhist sign of purity
food or gifts given to monks and nuns
